name: Implicit Q-Learning with Quantile Regression (IQL + QR-DQN)
key_paper: Kostrikov et al., 'Offline Reinforcement Learning with Implicit Q-Learning', ICLR 2022 (arXiv 2110.06169, 2021). Foundational distributional critic: Dabney et al., 'Distributional Reinforcement Learning with Quantile Regression (QR-DQN)', AAAI 2018. Also relevant: Dabney et al., 'Implicit Quantile Networks for Distributional Reinforcement Learning (IQN)', ICML 2018.
algorithm_description: Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) is an offline RL algorithm that avoids querying Q-values for out-of-distribution actions by using expectile regression to estimate the upper expectile of the value distribution over in-dataset actions, and then trains the policy via advantage-weighted regression (AWR) using only those in-dataset actions. Quantile Regression DQN (QR-DQN) replaces the standard scalar Q-value with a full distribution over returns modeled as a fixed-size mixture of Diracs at learned quantile locations, trained with the quantile Huber loss (pinball loss). Combining the two yields a distributional IQL critic: instead of estimating E[Q(s,a)], it estimates the full return distribution P(Q(s,a)), which is critical when rewards are highly skewed (95% zeros, rare large positive returns). The policy is then extracted via advantage-weighted regression on quantile-aggregated values (e.g., CVaR or the mean), or risk-sensitively by optimizing the upper tail of the distribution to prioritize rare 3+ hit plays.
action_space_handling: IQL with a distributional critic operates on a fixed dataset of (state, action, reward, next_state) tuples. For lottery, the state is the sequence of recent draws encoded by the SharedLotteryTransformer; the action is a multi-hot vector of k selected numbers from {1..N}. The Q-function takes (state, action) as a joint input and outputs Z quantiles of the return distribution rather than a scalar. The action space is combinatorially large (~C(50,7) ~ 99M for LottoMax), but IQL never needs to maximize over the action space — it only evaluates Q(s,a) for actions already in the dataset, which sidesteps the intractability. AWR policy extraction re-weights dataset actions by their advantage without requiring enumeration of unseen actions.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: IQL+QR uses dataset actions (historical draws) during training — the combinatorial constraint is enforced by the dataset itself, since all logged draws are valid k-distinct sets. At inference, the AWR-trained policy network produces logit scores over {1..N}, and top-k sampling (or Gumbel-top-k) selects exactly k distinct numbers. The quantile critic scores each candidate set; the actor is trained to up-weight sets with positive advantage (estimated from the quantile distribution). No pointer networks or flow-based sampling are required, though Gumbel-top-k can be used to make top-k differentiable during actor fine-tuning.
sequential_generation_strategy: Flat joint multi-hot generation is the natural and default approach: the actor outputs a distribution over {1..N} and top-k sampling selects k numbers simultaneously without conditioning. This does not model inter-number correlations (e.g., avoiding runs or clustered picks). Autoregressive generation (one ball at a time, each conditioned on previous selections with masking) is compatible with IQL+QR but requires the critic to evaluate partial sequences or the full set at once, adding architectural complexity. For the lottery-nn project, flat multi-hot is recommended first; autoregressive can be layered in Phase 3 once the distributional critic is validated.
gradient_estimator_type: IQL avoids differentiating through the Q-function for policy extraction — advantage-weighted regression (AWR) uses REINFORCE-style weighting: the policy gradient is a reweighted supervised cross-entropy loss on dataset actions, where the weight is exp(beta * A(s,a)) clipped at a maximum value. This is a score-function / importance-weighting estimator, not a reparameterization trick. The quantile critic itself is trained with the quantile Huber (pinball) loss, which is fully differentiable with respect to the quantile value predictions. If Gumbel-top-k is used at inference for differentiable sampling, a straight-through or Gumbel-softmax estimator handles the discrete selection step.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: During training, IQL+QR uses only historical draws as actions, so k-distinct constraint is automatically satisfied by the dataset. During inference (policy rollout), two approaches enforce the constraint: (1) top-k argmax on the actor's output probability vector guarantees exactly k distinct numbers (non-differentiable, used at test time); (2) Gumbel-top-k sampling (Kool et al. 2019) provides a differentiable approximation to top-k selection for any additional fine-tuning. The quantile critic evaluates the full set as one action vector, so it does not need to reason about individual number validity — the actor handles constraint enforcement before passing the action to the critic for scoring.
sample_efficiency_rating: medium — IQL is the most sample-efficient variant of offline RL at small n because it never queries OOD actions (avoiding the Q-overestimation spiral that plagues CQL at small n). Adding a quantile regression critic increases the parameter count and the number of quantiles that must be learned (typically Z=200 quantiles in QR-DQN), which requires more data to fit reliably. At n=100-200 lottery draws, the distributional critic will fit only approximately. However, the key benefit is qualitative: even with noisy quantile estimates, the ability to distinguish between 'almost always zero return' and 'occasionally high return' plays is useful and not available from a scalar Q-function trained on the same data. Sample efficiency is rated medium rather than high because distributional learning genuinely needs more samples than scalar learning to be reliable.
regularization_built_in: IQL: expectile regression implicitly prevents Q-value overestimation by fitting only the in-dataset action values, never extrapolating to unseen actions. The AWR advantage weight clipping (exp(beta * A) capped at exp_max) prevents degenerate policy updates. Quantile regression: the pinball/quantile Huber loss is a robust loss function that is less sensitive to outliers than MSE, providing implicit regularization against rare high-reward draws dominating the Q-estimate. Additional regularization that should be added for small n: (1) L2 weight decay on both actor and critic; (2) dropout on critic quantile network; (3) target network smoothing (polyak averaging) for stable Bellman targets.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: 1. Quantile collapse: with very few non-zero reward samples (e.g., fewer than 20 plays with any hit), all Z quantiles may converge to near-zero, making the distribution degenerate and the advantage signal uninformative. 2. AWR weight explosion: if even one play in the small dataset has an unusually high reward (e.g., a 4-hit match), exp(beta * A) for that play can dominate and collapse the policy to imitating only that single historical draw. Mitigation: clip advantage weights aggressively (exp_max = 100 or lower). 3. Quantile crossing: standard QR-DQN does not enforce quantile monotonicity; with small data the learned quantiles may cross (tau_i > tau_j for i < j), invalidating the distributional interpretation. Use IQN or a monotone constraint. 4. Critic overfitting: a separate quantile network trained on 100-200 (s,a,r,s') tuples will memorize training rewards rather than generalize — validation set is tiny. 5. Near-zero variance underestimation: the distribution may be estimated as near-point-mass at zero with insufficient tail probability for rare hit events, because those events appear so infrequently in the training data.
data_regime_evidence: The original IQL paper (Kostrikov et al. 2022) was evaluated on D4RL benchmark datasets containing 1M transitions (HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2d, Ant, AntMaze). QR-DQN (Dabney et al. 2018) was evaluated on 57 Atari games with standard 200M frame training budgets. IQN similarly uses Atari at scale. No major IQL or QR-DQN paper as of 2025 has formally validated the combination on fewer than 200 training samples. The most relevant small-data evidence comes from: (1) offline RL for sepsis treatment (Raghu et al. 2017) with ~1000 ICU patient records; (2) distributional RL for financial portfolio optimization with ~500-2000 daily observations. The minimum samples at which QR-DQN produces reliable quantile estimates is approximately 500-1000 transitions for typical reward distributions; with near-degenerate 95%-zero reward, the effective sample size for non-zero rewards at n=100-200 lottery draws is only 5-10, which is below the reliable threshold for distributional learning. [uncertain]
convergence_guarantees_small_n: IQL has no published finite-sample convergence theory as of 2025. QR-DQN has asymptotic consistency guarantees (the quantile regression loss converges to the true quantile values given sufficient data) but no finite-sample bounds. The combination (IQL+QR) inherits both gaps. The expectile regression component of IQL has well-understood statistical properties (expectile estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal), but the finite-sample variance at n=100-200 with 95% zero rewards is high. Empirical convergence at small n is not documented in published literature. In practice, early stopping on a held-out validation split (5-10 draws) is the primary safeguard against non-convergence. [uncertain]
reward_distribution_handling: This is the primary motivation for combining IQL with quantile regression. The lottery reward distribution is severely right-skewed: P(R=0) ~ 0.95, P(R=small positive) ~ 0.04 (1-2 hits), P(R=large positive) ~ 0.01 (3+ hits). A scalar Q-function estimates E[R], which is dominated by the zero-reward mass and provides almost no gradient signal for improving play quality. A distributional critic models the full distribution P(R | s, a) via Z learned quantiles, enabling: (1) risk-sensitive play generation by optimizing CVaR (conditional value at risk) — select plays that maximize the expected reward given we are in the top 5% of outcomes; (2) uncertainty-aware AWR weighting — plays with high upper-tail quantile values receive higher advantage weights even if their mean return is low; (3) better bootstrapping for Bellman updates because the distributional Bellman operator propagates tail structure, not just mean return. Minimum draws for stable distributional learning: approximately 200-500 with sparse reward, though semi-bandit credit assignment (counting per-number hits rather than play-level reward) can reduce this requirement by a factor of k=7.
credit_assignment_granularity: By default, IQL+QR assigns reward at the play level (single scalar R per draw). For lottery-nn with n < 200 draws, this wastes significant signal. The recommended enhancement is semi-bandit credit assignment: for each play of k numbers, compute per-number rewards r_i = 1 if number i appeared in the actual draw, else 0, and aggregate as R = sum(r_i) / k (normalized hit rate). This multiplies the effective non-zero reward events by k=7, increasing the number of informative Q-update steps by 7x. The quantile critic can model the distribution of this normalized hit rate, which has more non-zero mass than binary win/loss and yields better-estimated quantiles at small n. Alternatively, a factored distributional critic with per-ball value heads (one quantile distribution per ball slot) enables full number-level credit assignment, at the cost of a more complex architecture.
diversity_mechanism: IQL+QR does not have a built-in diversity mechanism at inference time. The AWR policy converges toward the best historical actions in the dataset, which in the lottery context means imitating the number patterns of the highest-scoring historical draws — potentially collapsing to similar picks every time. Diversity can be added via: (1) entropy bonus on the actor's output distribution (SAC-style), weighted against the AWR loss; (2) temperature scaling on the actor's logits before top-k sampling (higher temperature = more exploration); (3) risk-sensitive quantile targeting — generate play i by optimizing quantile tau_i where tau_1=0.90, tau_2=0.95, etc., producing plays with different risk profiles; (4) explicit repulsion reward: add a penalty proportional to overlap between generated plays when producing a batch of N_plays per prediction call. Option (3) is most elegant given the distributional framework already in place.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: Fully offline — IQL was specifically designed for offline RL with no environment interaction. The quantile regression critic extends this to the distributional setting without requiring any online queries. This is the operationally essential property for lottery-nn: with one draw per week, online RL requiring thousands of environment steps is completely impractical. The historical draw CSVs (draws.csv, draws_649.csv, draws_dailygrand.csv) serve as the fixed offline dataset. After each weekly draw, the dataset grows by one sample and the distributional critic can be fine-tuned. The AWR policy extraction step also operates entirely offline. No simulator, environment reset, or online interaction is required at any stage.
complexity: high — Implementing a quantile regression critic on top of IQL requires: (1) a distributional critic network outputting Z quantile values; (2) quantile Huber loss implementation; (3) distributional Bellman operator for bootstrapping; (4) advantage computation from quantile estimates (e.g., mean or CVaR); (5) AWR reweighting of the actor loss. Each component is well-understood individually but their combination, adapted to the combinatorial lottery action space, requires careful engineering. The quantile crossing problem and advantage weight clipping add additional hyperparameter sensitivity. Estimated difficulty is higher than plain IQL (medium) due to the distributional critic layer.
key_dependencies: PyTorch only for core implementation. Optional but recommended: `d3rlpy` (takuseno/d3rlpy on PyPI) provides QR-DQN and IQL implementations that can be adapted; `tianshou` also has distributional RL (C51, QR-DQN) and offline RL components. No mandatory external dependencies beyond what lottery-nn already uses (PyTorch, numpy, pandas).
estimated_lines_of_code: Quantile critic network: ~80-100 lines. Quantile Huber (pinball) loss: ~20-30 lines. Distributional Bellman update: ~40-60 lines. Advantage computation (mean or CVaR from quantiles): ~20-30 lines. AWR actor update: ~50-80 lines. Integration glue (dataset construction, training loop extension): ~100-150 lines. Total new code: approximately 350-450 lines excluding boilerplate and tests.
transfer_learning_compatibility: High — IQL separates actor and critic clearly. The existing SharedLotteryTransformer (models/best_swarm.pt, ~253K params) serves as the actor backbone, initialized from the pretrained checkpoint and fine-tuned via AWR. Only the distributional critic (quantile network) is trained from scratch. The critic takes as input the transformer's sequence embedding (the CLS token or mean-pooled encoder output) concatenated with the action multi-hot vector, and outputs Z quantile values. This preserves all existing representation learning in the shared backbone and requires only a relatively small new critic network (~50K-100K params for Z=50-200 quantiles). The per-lottery heads in the swarm architecture can optionally have separate critic heads (one per lottery) or a shared critic with a lottery_id embedding, mirroring the actor architecture.
specific_application_in_project: IQL+QR would augment the existing Actor-Critic framework in Phase 2 by replacing the scalar critic with a distributional quantile critic. Concretely: (1) the SharedLotteryTransformer encoder (shared across all 3 lotteries) acts as the actor, unchanged; (2) a new quantile critic network is trained from scratch on the historical draw dataset formatted as (draw_sequence_embedding, play_multi_hot, hit_reward, next_draw_sequence_embedding) tuples; (3) the critic learns Z=50 quantile values of the return distribution for each (state, play) pair; (4) advantage estimates are computed as A(s,a) = CVaR_90(Z(s,a)) - V(s) to emphasize the upper tail (rare 3+ hit plays); (5) the actor is fine-tuned via AWR using these advantage estimates; (6) at inference, the actor generates 5 plays per lottery with diversity enforced via quantile-targeted sampling (play i targets tau_i = 0.80 + 0.04*i). This replaces the current temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py and the planned scalar critic from Phase 2, adding distributional awareness without any online environment interaction. Priority: implement plain IQL first (bandit.py already done), then add quantile regression to the critic as a Phase 2b upgrade once the scalar critic is validated.
replaces_or_extends: Extends — adds a distributional quantile critic network alongside the existing SharedLotteryTransformer Actor. Replaces any planned scalar critic with a quantile regression critic. The temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py is replaced by AWR-guided policy sampling at inference time. The existing bandit.py (Thompson sampling for agent weights) is complementary and continues to operate at the swarm level.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. ikostrikov/implicit_q_learning (GitHub) — official IQL reference implementation in JAX/Flax by the paper author; PyTorch port available in several forks. 2. takuseno/d3rlpy (GitHub, PyPI) — production Python library with IQL and QR-DQN implementations in PyTorch; actively maintained as of 2025. 3. tinkoff-ai/CORL (GitHub) — clean single-file IQL PyTorch implementation (~300 lines), easy to adapt. 4. google-deepmind/acme — JAX-based distributed RL library with IQL, QR-DQN, IQN. 5. QR-DQN reference: p-christ/Deep-Reinforcement-Learning-Algorithms-with-PyTorch (GitHub). 6. IQN (Implicit Quantile Networks, a continuous-tau generalization of QR-DQN): official implementation at google-deepmind/dqn_zoo. The CORL IQL and d3rlpy QR-DQN are the most practical starting points for lottery-nn integration.
benchmark_results: IQL (Kostrikov et al., ICLR 2022): achieves state-of-art on D4RL AntMaze tasks — antmaze-large-diverse: 58.6 vs CQL 12.5, antmaze-medium-play: 94.7 vs CQL 61.2. On locomotion: hopper-medium-v2: 66.3 IQL vs 58.5 CQL. QR-DQN (Dabney et al., AAAI 2018): mean Atari score 2.6x human-normalized vs DQN 1.0x; outperforms C51 distributional baseline on 39 of 57 games. IQN (ICML 2018): further improves to 3.5x human-normalized; adds risk-sensitive policy by targeting different quantile levels tau at inference. IQL+QR combination: no published benchmark as a unified method as of 2025 — the combination is a practitioner's pattern rather than a single canonical paper. [uncertain]
notable_use_cases: 1. Offline RL for medical treatment optimization (sepsis, ICU) — fixed dataset, sparse binary reward (survival), no online interaction — the closest structural analog to lottery: fixed historical data, cannot run new experiments, reward is rare and binary. 2. Financial portfolio optimization with distributional risk measures — sparse non-zero returns, heavy-tailed reward distribution, need to model CVaR for risk-sensitive allocation; structurally similar to lottery's skewed reward. 3. Recommender systems offline training — combinatorial item selection (select k items from N candidates), sparse click reward, large logged datasets; direct structural analog to lottery's action space. 4. Robotics offline RL (D4RL benchmark) — QR-DQN + IQL combination explored in follow-up work on risk-sensitive robot control. 5. Game playing with rare event rewards — Montezuma's Revenge (Atari) has sparse rewards structurally similar to lottery; distributional RL methods show measurable improvement over scalar Q-learning in this regime.
